title: Solar Farm Developers
one_liner: Utility-scale solar developers turn land, permits, interconnection rights, tax credits, equipment procurement and construction execution into grid-scale power assets.
overview: Solar farm developers originate, permit, finance, engineer, procure and build ground-mounted utility-scale photovoltaic projects, often adding battery storage and then selling power under utility, corporate or merchant offtake structures. The baseline IBISWorld file framed the industry as a utility-scale construction and development business with 2021 revenue of $11.4 billion, a 2021 profit margin of 6.1%, low concentration, high capital intensity and heavy dependence on federal tax credits, state renewable standards and equipment costs. By 2025-2026, the industry’s physical deployment scale had moved well beyond the 2021 baseline: SEIA/Wood Mackenzie reported 34.7 GWdc of utility-scale solar installed in 2025, down 16% from 2024 after delayed Q4 commercial operation dates, while EIA reported 27.2 GW of utility-scale solar added in 2025 and 43.4 GW planned for 2026. Using DOE’s 2024Q1 utility-scale modeled market price of $1.12/Wdc as a construction-value proxy, 2025 utility-scale installations imply roughly $38.9 billion of installed project value, though pure developer revenue is smaller because ownership, EPC, equipment and financing margins are split across the project stack.

key_stats.market_size: 2025: about $38.9 billion implied US utility-scale solar farm installed project value, calculated as 34.7 GWdc installed in 2025 multiplied by DOE 2024Q1 utility-scale PV modeled market price of $1.12/Wdc.
key_stats.growth: 2025: utility-scale solar installations fell 16% year over year to 34.7 GWdc; 2026: EIA reported developers planned 43.4 GW of new utility-scale solar capacity, 60% more than 2025 utility-scale additions on EIA’s AC/grid basis.
key_stats.installed_capacity: 2025: SEIA/Wood Mackenzie reported 34.7 GWdc of US utility-scale solar installed; EIA reported 27.2 GW of utility-scale solar added to the US grid in 2025.
key_stats.planned_capacity: 2026: EIA reported 43.4 GW of planned US utility-scale solar additions, equal to 51% of all planned new utility-scale electric generating capacity.
key_stats.cost_benchmark: 2024Q1: DOE benchmarked a representative 100 MWdc utility-scale PV system at $0.98/Wdc minimum sustainable price, $1.12/Wdc modeled market price, $19/kWdc-year O&M and $47/MWh unsubsidized benchmark LCOE.
key_stats.manufacturing_capacity: 2025: SEIA/Wood Mackenzie reported US solar module manufacturing capacity of 65.5 GW, up from 42.5 GW at year-end 2024.
key_stats.market_concentration: 2025: Cleanview tracked 503 US utility-scale solar developers, 4,081 projects and 467,783 MW of combined development pipeline.

baseline_2022.market_size: 2022: $20.3 billion US solar EPC market size in Global Market Insights’ broader US EPC series; the baseline IBISWorld file’s narrow solar farm developer revenue implied about $11.6 billion for 2022 if its 2021-2026 forecast CAGR of 1.4% is applied to 2021 revenue of $11.4 billion.
baseline_2022.growth: 2022: baseline forecast growth was about 1.4% for the narrow IBISWorld solar farm developer revenue series; broader US solar EPC revenue rose sharply from 2022 to 2023, from $20.3 billion to $32.7 billion, as post-IRA utility-scale and distributed solar activity accelerated.
baseline_2022.context: 2022 is a policy break year because the Inflation Reduction Act was enacted on August 16, 2022, extending and reshaping clean-energy tax incentives that materially improved the development pipeline after the 2021 baseline report.

how_it_makes_money: Developers earn development fees, EPC or construction-management margins, gains from selling shovel-ready or operating projects, sponsor equity returns, tax-credit monetization economics, power-purchase agreement spreads, merchant or hedge revenues, operations and maintenance contracts and, increasingly, storage co-development revenue. Larger firms may retain ownership of projects, while smaller developers often monetize projects at notice-to-proceed, financial close or commercial operation.

cost_structure.equipment: 2024-2025: modules, inverters, trackers, racking, transformers, switchgear and optional batteries are the largest controllable project costs; DOE’s benchmark cost categories include module, inverter, storage, structural BOS and electrical BOS.
cost_structure.labor_and_fieldwork: 2024-2025: civil, electrical, mechanical installation, commissioning and project-management labor are material costs, especially as projects become larger, more remote and more storage-heavy.
cost_structure.interconnection_and_grid: 2025-2026: interconnection studies, network upgrades, transformer lead times, transmission constraints and congestion-management costs remain major schedule and capital risks.
cost_structure.land_and_permitting: 2025-2026: land leases, site control, environmental studies, local taxes, legal work and federal, state and county permitting costs are rising pain points, especially for projects on or near federally affected land.
cost_structure.financing_and_tax: 2025-2026: interest expense, sponsor equity, tax-credit transfer discounts, tax-equity structuring, safe-harbor equipment procurement and compliance work are central to project economics.
cost_structure.profit: 2021 baseline: IBISWorld reported a 6.1% industry profit margin; 2025-2026 margins vary widely by project timing, tax-credit eligibility, interconnection cost allocation and equipment procurement strategy.

current_dynamics: The market is demand-rich but execution-constrained. Data centers, electrification, utility resource plans and corporate PPAs support new procurement, while developers are adapting to tighter tax-credit timelines, Foreign Entity of Concern sourcing rules, tariff exposure, federal permitting reviews, local opposition and grid-connection bottlenecks. SEIA reported 2025 utility-scale installations declined 16% despite stable full-year contracted volumes and stronger financial-close and interconnection indicators. In 2026, EIA’s planned 43.4 GW utility-scale solar additions show a rebound pipeline, with Texas accounting for 40% of planned new utility-scale solar capacity.
whats_growing: Utility-scale solar paired with battery storage; Texas, Arizona, Michigan and other high-load-growth markets; corporate and data-center offtake; safe-harbored equipment strategies; domestic module, cell and wafer capacity; tracker-based crystalline silicon systems; project acquisitions by large sponsors with balance-sheet and tax-credit capacity.
whats_shrinking: Late-stage 2025 commercial operation urgency after tax-credit timing changes; community solar installations in mature markets such as Maine and New York; projects exposed to unresolved federal permitting, local siting opposition, high network-upgrade costs or uncertain FEOC compliance; pure fixed-tilt and thin-film niches where crystalline silicon tracker projects dominate new capacity.
recent_developments: 2025: SEIA/Wood Mackenzie reported 43.2 GWdc of total US solar installed, down 14% from 2024, with solar representing 54% of new US generating capacity.
2025: Utility-scale solar installed 34.7 GWdc, down 16% from 2024, as many Q4 projects delayed commercial operation dates and developers shifted toward safe-harbor strategies.
2025: US solar module manufacturing capacity reached 65.5 GW, up from 42.5 GW at year-end 2024, though actual domestic production remained below demand.
2026-02-12: Treasury and IRS issued Notice 2026-15 guidance on prohibited foreign entity material-assistance rules for clean electricity and manufacturing tax credits.
2026-02-20: EIA reported developers planned 43.4 GW of new US utility-scale solar capacity in 2026, a 60% increase from 2025 utility-scale additions if realized.
2026-06-10: SEIA reported 7.8 GW of new US solar capacity in Q1 2026 and said utility-scale solar contracts rose 15% year over year, supported by AI-driven electricity demand.
outlook: The 2026-2030 outlook is cautiously positive: near-term construction should be supported by projects delayed from 2025, safe-harbored pipelines and urgent load growth, but the industry is unlikely to grow smoothly. EIA’s 43.4 GW planned 2026 utility-scale solar additions point to a large rebound year, while SEIA/Wood Mackenzie’s 2025 Year in Review expects average utility-scale builds of about 35 GWdc annually through 2030 and 381 GWdc of utility-scale additions over the 10-year outlook. The strongest developers will be those that can control interconnection risk, qualify projects for tax credits under evolving FEOC rules, secure bankable offtake, procure domestic or compliant equipment and pair solar with storage where grid value is highest.
themes: Solar-plus-storage as the default utility-scale product
one_sentence: The US solar farm development market remains large and strategically important in 2026, but growth is being pulled between surging power demand from electrification and data centers, and policy, permitting, interconnection and supply-chain uncertainty.

title: Solar Panel Installation
one_liner: Solar panel installers convert residential and small commercial demand for lower electric bills, resiliency and tax incentives into rooftop and onsite PV projects.
overview: Operators design, sell, permit and install photovoltaic systems for homeowners and non-utility commercial customers, often coordinating panels, inverters, batteries, racking, interconnection and inspection. The 2022 IBIS baseline described a fragmented, fast-grown contractor industry centered on residential installations, with 2022 revenue of $11.374 billion and 13,402 establishments. By 2025, demand was still supported by high retail electricity rates and cheaper PV equipment, but installers faced a tougher financing and policy environment: the US solar industry installed 43.2 GWdc in 2025, down 14% from 2024, while residential capacity slipped 2% to 4,647 MWdc and commercial capacity rose 6% to 2,345 MWdc. The industry remains labor-intensive and local-permit-heavy, with national brands competing against thousands of regional electrical, roofing and solar contractors.

key_stats.market_size: $14.9 billion US Solar Panel Installation revenue in 2025
key_stats.growth: 2.9% revenue CAGR over 2020-2025; total US solar capacity additions fell 14% year over year in 2025 to 43.2 GWdc
key_stats.installed_capacity: 43.2 GWdc of US solar capacity installed in 2025; residential 4,647 MWdc in 2025, down 2%; commercial 2,345 MWdc in 2025, up 6%; community solar 1,435 MWdc in 2025, down 25%
key_stats.employment: BLS reported 28,600 solar photovoltaic installer jobs in 2024 and projected 42% occupational growth from 2024 to 2034
key_stats.wages: BLS reported $51,860 median annual pay for solar photovoltaic installers in May 2024
key_stats.market_structure: IBIS baseline showed 13,402 establishments and 13,299 enterprises in 2022, indicating a low-concentration contractor market

baseline_2022.growth: 1.6% revenue growth in 2022 and -0.2% annualized revenue change from 2017 to 2022
baseline_2022.profit: $705 million profit in 2022, equal to a 6.2% profit margin
baseline_2022.segments: 2022 revenue mix: residential installation 67.9%, commercial installation 22.2%, other nonresidential installation 9.9%; product mix: silicon cell panel installation 69.0%, thin-film panel installation 23.4%, other 7.6%

how_it_makes_money: Installers earn project revenue from site assessment, system design, permitting, equipment procurement, mounting, electrical work, utility interconnection and final inspection. Residential jobs are sold as cash purchases, loans, leases or power purchase agreements; third-party-owned models let installers and finance partners monetize tax credits, long-term customer payments, SRECs and sometimes battery/grid-services value. Commercial jobs are larger and more bid-driven, with revenue tied to EPC contracts, roof or ground-mount complexity, prevailing-wage requirements, interconnection timelines and equipment availability.
cost_structure: Major costs are PV modules, inverters, batteries, racking, wiring and balance-of-system materials; field labor and subcontracted electrical/roofing work; sales commissions, customer acquisition and financing fees; vehicles, tools, insurance and permitting; and warranty/service obligations. The 2022 baseline showed $2.567 billion in wages and a 6.2% profit margin, and 2025-2026 margins remain sensitive to module tariffs, interest rates, cancellation rates, installation throughput and rework after inspection failures.
major_players: Sunrun: largest US residential solar installer in 2025, with 12.7% annual residential market share and 8,404 MW of networked solar capacity at December 31, 2025
Freedom Forever: second-largest US residential solar installer in 2025, with 6.1% annual residential market share
Tesla Energy: important residential solar, Powerwall and inverter competitor; Tesla reported $12.270 billion in 2025 energy generation and storage sales
SunPower Inc. / Complete Solaria: acquired selected SunPower Corporation assets in September 2024 and operated under the SunPower brand in 2025-2026
Regional electrical, roofing and solar contractors: collectively hold most installations because the 2022 IBIS baseline had more than 13,000 enterprises and low concentration
current_dynamics: The market is no longer a simple volume-growth story. In 2025, installers benefited from a late residential rush before the Section 25D credit cutoff, but the full-year residential market still declined 2% as financing stress, module shortages and delivery delays limited completions. Commercial solar performed better in 2025 because California NEM 2.0 legacy projects continued coming online, while community solar contracted 25%. Tariff actions on cells and modules from Cambodia, Malaysia, Thailand and Vietnam raised procurement risk in 2025, and IRS guidance under OBBBA added deadline pressure for 2026 project planning. High retail power prices, battery attachment, backup-power demand and third-party ownership are offsetting some of the pressure from weaker customer-owned residential economics.
whats_growing: Commercial onsite solar, battery-paired residential systems, third-party-owned residential offerings, grid-services-ready systems, Puerto Rico residential demand, domestic module supply relationships and installer service revenue for monitoring, repairs and storage retrofits are growing in 2025-2026. BLS also projects solar PV installer employment to grow 42% from 2024 to 2034, reflecting long-term labor demand despite near-term residential volatility.
whats_shrinking: Customer-owned residential solar is shrinking after the 2025 expiration of the Section 25D credit, with SEIA/Wood Mackenzie expecting residential installations to contract 19% in 2026. Community solar fell 25% in 2025 as Maine and New York pipelines cooled. Highly leveraged residential finance platforms weakened in 2024-2025, including SunPower Corporation's August 2024 bankruptcy and Sunnova's June 2025 Chapter 11 filing. Small installers without secured module supply are more exposed to 2025-2026 equipment constraints and tariff-driven price volatility.
recent_developments: 2024-08-05: SunPower Corporation filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy, reshaping a major residential installer brand.
2025-04-21: US Commerce issued final affirmative AD/CVD determinations on crystalline PV cells from Cambodia, Malaysia, Thailand and Vietnam.
2025-05-20: USITC found US industry injury or threat of injury, clearing the way for AD/CVD orders on solar cell imports from the four Southeast Asian countries.
2025-06-08: Sunnova Energy International filed voluntary Chapter 11 petitions to pursue asset sales while continuing system servicing.
2025-07-04: OBBBA accelerated clean-energy credit terminations, including ending the Section 25D residential clean energy credit after 2025.
2026-03-20: EIA reported utility-scale solar generated 296,000 GWh in 2025, up 34% from 2024, and small-scale solar generated 93,000 GWh, up 11%.
outlook: The 2026 outlook is mixed: residential installers face a down year as the 30% customer-owned federal credit disappears, while third-party ownership, batteries, commercial retrofits and high electric bills keep demand from collapsing. Commercial and larger distributed projects should remain healthier where owners can still structure eligible tax-credit financing, but 2026 procurement decisions will be shaped by FEOC rules, safe-harbor timing and AD/CVD tariffs. Over the medium term, declining equipment costs, rising electricity demand and the normalization of solar-plus-storage should return the industry to growth, though revenue gains may be uneven and more concentrated among installers with strong financing channels, supply contracts and service capabilities.
themes: Trade policy and module sourcing risk

title: Solar Panel Manufacturing in the US
one_liner: US solar panel manufacturing is scaling rapidly under tax credits, tariffs and utility demand, but domestic cell, wafer and polysilicon capacity still trails module assembly.
overview: Operators manufacture photovoltaic modules and cells in the United States for residential, commercial, community-solar and utility-scale buyers. The 2022 baseline industry was still small and volatile, with 2022 revenue of $5.17 billion and a 2022 decline of 5.3%, but policy support and trade protection have since changed the operating environment. In 2025, US solar installations totaled 43.1 GWdc and the broader US solar market was valued at $69.1 billion, while domestic module manufacturing capacity expanded sharply to 65.5 GW by year-end 2025. The key constraint in 2026 is not module assembly capacity alone, but whether US producers can ramp cells, wafers, ingots, glass, polysilicon and qualified non-foreign-entity-of-concern supply fast enough to support domestic-content demand.

key_stats.market_size: 2025 estimated US solar panel manufacturing revenue: about $6.1 billion, derived from the 2022 IBIS baseline of $5.17 billion and its 2022-2027 projected CAGR of 5.9%.
key_stats.growth: 2022-2027 projected revenue CAGR: 5.9%; 2025 US solar installations declined 14% year over year to 43.1 GWdc after the 2024 record year.
key_stats.module_capacity: 2025 year-end US solar module manufacturing capacity: 65.5 GW, up from 42.5 GW at year-end 2024.
key_stats.demand_indicator: 2026 planned US utility-scale solar additions: 43.4 GW, 60% above 2025 utility-scale additions if realized.
key_stats.jobs_indicator: 2026 Q1 US solar jobs across the broader solar industry: 280,119; 2025 value of broader US solar market: $69.1 billion.

how_it_makes_money: Manufacturers sell solar modules and cells to project developers, installers, utilities, commercial buyers and distributors. Revenue comes mainly from silicon modules and cells, thin-film modules and cells, and smaller specialty module categories. In 2025-2026, additional economics come from long-term utility offtake contracts, domestic-content premiums, Section 45X advanced manufacturing production credits, and the ability to offer tariff-resilient US-made supply.
cost_structure: Major costs are polysilicon or CdTe semiconductor materials, solar glass, frames or backrails, encapsulants, backsheets, junction boxes, factory equipment, depreciation, energy, freight and skilled labor. The 2022 baseline showed profit at 7.5% of revenue and wages at $372.4 million; in 2025-2026, margins depend heavily on utilization, cell sourcing, tariff exposure, tax-credit monetization, automation and whether plants can ramp without quality or yield losses.
current_dynamics: Domestic module capacity now looks large enough on paper to serve much of annual US demand, but production remains below nameplate capacity and the silicon supply chain is uneven. First Solar leads in US thin-film CdTe manufacturing, Qcells is scaling vertically integrated silicon production in Georgia, and T1 Energy is ramping Texas module output while building cell capacity. Trade policy is central: AD/CVD orders on Southeast Asian cells and modules, Section 301 tariffs on China-linked solar inputs, and new 2026 Section 232 tariff and price-floor actions support domestic manufacturers but raise uncertainty for developers dependent on imported components.
whats_growing: US module assembly, thin-film CdTe output, domestic-content-qualified modules, utility-scale procurement, solar recycling, automation, and new cell/wafer/ingot capacity are growing. Qcells expects 8.6 GW of US output by Q3 2026, First Solar expects more than 14 GW of US annual capacity in 2026, and T1 Energy guides to 3.1-4.2 GW of 2026 module production from G1 Dallas.
whats_shrinking: Pure reliance on low-cost imported Southeast Asian modules is shrinking as 2025 AD/CVD orders hit Cambodia, Malaysia, Thailand and Vietnam. Residential installation volume is also pressured by tax-credit changes and financing costs, while manufacturers without domestic-content advantages, scale, automation or secure cell supply face margin and utilization pressure.
recent_developments: 2025-04-21: The US Department of Commerce issued final affirmative AD/CVD determinations on crystalline solar cells from Cambodia, Malaysia, Thailand and Vietnam.
2025-05-20: The USITC found US industry injury or threat of injury from solar cell and module imports from Cambodia, Malaysia, Thailand and Vietnam, clearing the way for AD/CVD orders.
2025-12-31: SEIA reported that 2025 US solar installations totaled 43.1 GWdc, down 14% from 2024, while US module capacity reached 65.5 GW by year-end 2025.
2026-03-31: T1 Energy reported 2.79 GW of 2025 module production at G1 Dallas and guided to 3.1-4.2 GW of 2026 production.
2026-06-09: Qcells began solar cell manufacturing at Cartersville, Georgia, targeting 3.3 GW of ingot, wafer and cell capacity and 3.5 GW of module capacity at the site by Q3 2026.
2026-08-07: The Trump administration announced new Section 232 tariffs and minimum prices on imported polysilicon and solar components, effective December 4, 2026.
outlook: The 2026-2031 outlook is positive but uneven. Utility-scale demand and domestic-content procurement should support revenue growth, and 2026 planned utility-scale solar additions of 43.4 GW create a strong demand backdrop. The industry’s upside depends on converting nameplate capacity into reliable output, expanding cells and wafers, keeping tax-credit eligibility, and preserving project economics despite tariffs. The main downside risks are policy reversals, delayed factory ramps, high interest rates, lower module prices from global oversupply, and developers deferring projects because trade compliance raises costs or delays procurement.
themes: Solar recycling and circular supply chains
one_sentence: In 2025-2026, the industry is shifting from a small, import-exposed module-and-cell base toward larger domestic module plants and the first meaningful US silicon supply-chain buildout in years.

title: Solar Water Heater Installation
one_liner: A small, fragmented specialty installation market tied to residential remodeling, new housing, energy prices and clean-energy tax credits.
overview: Operators install solar thermal water heating systems for homes, multifamily buildings, hotels, campuses, laundries and other properties with hot-water loads. The market is much smaller than rooftop solar PV because solar thermal systems compete directly with gas, electric and heat pump water heaters, require roof/plumbing integration and depend heavily on state incentives, solar exposure and local contractor availability. The 2021 IBISWorld baseline placed revenue at $318.1 million, with a 2021-2026 forecast of essentially flat revenue; current 2025-2026 signals point to a similar small-market profile but with a sharper policy overhang after the federal residential clean energy credit was terminated for property placed in service after December 31, 2025.

key_stats.market_size: 2026 estimated US installation revenue: about $316 million, based on the 2021 IBISWorld baseline forecast of $316.4 million for 2026 and current 2025-2026 demand signals.
key_stats.growth: 2021-2026 estimated CAGR: about -0.1% from the IBISWorld baseline forecast; 2026 demand risk is negative after the 2025 residential credit sunset.
key_stats.profit_margin: 2021 baseline profit margin: 6.5% of revenue; 2026 baseline forecast margin: 6.8%.
key_stats.employment: 2021 baseline employment: 1,531 workers; 2026 baseline forecast employment: 1,584 workers.
key_stats.housing_indicator: June 2026 US housing starts: 1.427 million SAAR, up 3.5% from June 2025; June 2026 permits: 1.367 million SAAR, down 2.3% from June 2025.
key_stats.energy_indicator: EIA July 2026 STEO forecast Henry Hub natural gas price: $3.53/MMBtu in 2025 and $3.67/MMBtu in 2026.
key_stats.product_availability: ENERGY STAR solar water heater certified model dataset listed 55 rows as of July 29, 2026.

baseline_2022.market_size: 2022 estimated revenue: about $317.8 million, derived from the 2021 IBISWorld revenue of $318.1 million and its 2021-2026 forecast CAGR of -0.11%.
baseline_2022.growth: 2022 estimated annual growth: about -0.1%, in line with the 2021 IBISWorld 2021-2026 forecast CAGR.
baseline_2022.context: The 2022 baseline still assumed continued tax-credit support, before the 2025 OBBB accelerated the residential clean energy credit termination.

how_it_makes_money: Installers earn project revenue from site assessment, permitting, roof or rack preparation, collector mounting, storage tank placement, pumps and controls, glycol loops or direct plumbing, backup-heater integration, commissioning and maintenance. Residential jobs dominate revenue, while commercial work comes from properties with large hot-water loads such as hotels, multifamily housing, campuses, laundries, hospitals and industrial process-heat users.
cost_structure: The 2021 baseline cost profile was labor-heavy and locally delivered: wages were about $80 million against $318.1 million of revenue, or roughly 25.1% of 2021 revenue; profit was $21 million, or 6.5% of 2021 revenue. Other major costs include collectors, tanks, pumps, heat exchangers, controls, copper or PEX piping, glycol, valves, permits, insurance, vehicles, subcontracted roofing or electrical work and customer acquisition. Active and closed-loop systems carry higher material and labor complexity than passive systems.
major_players: Fragmented local plumbing, HVAC, roofing and solar contractors with no dominant national installer in the 2021 baseline.
Solar marketing and project-originating firms that subcontract installation to licensed local contractors.
Equipment suppliers and certified-product brands, including solar thermal manufacturers and water-heater OEMs, influence channel availability but are not typically installation market-share leaders.
current_dynamics: In 2025, demand was pulled forward by the final year of the 30% residential clean energy credit for solar water heaters. In 2026, the same policy change becomes a headwind because residential systems placed in service after December 31, 2025 no longer qualify for the federal residential clean energy credit. Housing is mixed: June 2026 starts improved year over year, but permits declined, limiting visibility for new-construction installations. Natural gas prices are higher than 2024 levels but still moderate by historical shock standards, so fuel switching is helpful but not enough to make solar thermal a mass-market water-heating choice. Heat pump water heaters remain the main substitute because they are easier to specify indoors and are promoted through efficiency programs.
whats_growing: Commercial, multifamily and institutional applications with predictable daily hot-water loads are the most defensible growth areas in 2026. Closed-loop and active systems are favored where freeze protection, controls and larger tanks matter. State, utility and local rebate searches are more important after the 2025 federal residential credit sunset. Hybrid approaches that pair solar thermal with efficient backup systems or building decarbonization retrofits are gaining relevance.
whats_shrinking: Standalone residential retrofit demand is shrinking in 2026 where the loss of the federal 30% residential clean energy credit raises payback periods. Low-complexity passive systems remain geographically constrained to warmer climates. Small installers are also exposed to customer deferrals when mortgage rates, remodeling budgets or permit backlogs weaken project conversion.
recent_developments: 2022-08: The Inflation Reduction Act restored the residential clean energy credit to 30% for qualified solar water heating property installed from 2022 onward.
2025-07: Public Law 119-21 accelerated the residential clean energy credit termination, ending eligibility for solar water heaters after December 31, 2025.
2025: SEIA reported 43.1 GWdc of US solar capacity installed, down 14% from 2024, with residential solar nearly flat as installers rushed projects before credit expiration.
2026-06: Census reported June 2026 housing starts at 1.427 million SAAR, up 3.5% from June 2025, while permits fell 2.3% year over year.
2026-07: EIA forecast Henry Hub natural gas at $3.67/MMBtu for 2026 versus $3.53/MMBtu in 2025, with storage above the five-year average limiting price pressure.
2026-07: ENERGY STAR’s solar water heater dataset showed 55 certified model rows as of July 29, 2026.
outlook: The 2026 outlook is cautious. The industry should remain a niche specialty trade near the 2021 baseline forecast of roughly $316 million in annual revenue, but growth is likely weaker than it looked before the 2025 tax-law change. Demand should hold up best in sunny states with state or utility incentives and in commercial buildings where hot-water load is large enough to justify engineering and installation complexity. Residential installers will need to compete harder against heat pump water heaters and conventional replacements on installed cost, payback and simplicity.

one_sentence: US solar water heater installers remain a niche construction trade in 2026, with demand supported by energy-efficiency economics but pressured by lower-cost heat pump water heaters, modest housing activity and the post-2025 end of the residential clean energy credit.

title: Soy & Almond Milk Production
one_liner: A mature but still strategically important plant-based dairy segment where retail plant-based milk sales softened in 2025 while foodservice, soy revival, protein-fortified products and cafe channels kept demand alive.
overview: Soy & Almond Milk Production sits inside the broader plant-based milk market. The 2022 IBIS baseline described a fast-growing, highly concentrated manufacturing industry led by Danone North America and Blue Diamond Growers, with almond milk overtaking soy milk as the main revenue source. By 2025, the category had matured: GFI/SPINS reported US plant-based milk retail dollar sales of $2.7 billion in 2025, down 2% from 2024, with unit sales down 5%, but the category still held 13% of total retail milk dollar sales and had the highest household penetration among plant-based categories at 38% of US households. Foodservice was a brighter channel in 2025, with plant-based milk dollar sales up 16% and pound sales up 14%, supported by coffee and tea usage and the removal of plant-based milk surcharges at some chains. The operating story in 2026 is therefore less about early-stage adoption and more about defending shelf space, improving taste and nutrition, managing almond and soybean input costs, and finding growth in protein, simple-label, organic, barista and foodservice formats.

key_stats.market_size: 2025 US retail plant-based milk sales: $2.7 billion; almond milk sales were about $1.6 billion in 2025 according to Statista category text.
key_stats.growth: 2025 US retail plant-based milk dollar sales: -2% year over year; 2025 unit sales: -5% year over year.
key_stats.market_share: 2025 plant-based milk share of total US retail milk dollar sales: 13%; 2025 natural-channel share: 30%.
key_stats.household_penetration: 2025 plant-based milk household penetration: 38% of US households; 75% of buying households purchased more than once.
key_stats.foodservice_growth: 2025 US foodservice plant-based milk dollar sales: +16%; pound sales: +14%; pound share of foodservice milk: 13%.
key_stats.input_cost_signals: 2026 California almond crop forecast: 2.7 billion pounds, down 1% from 2025; 2026/27 US soybean production forecast: record 4.5 billion bushels; 2026/27 soybean season-average farm price forecast: $11.40 per bushel.

baseline_2022.market_size: 2022 projected industry revenue: about $2.83 billion, inferred from the Jan. 2022 IBISWorld baseline of $2.766 billion in 2021 revenue and a 2021-2027 projected CAGR of 2.14%.
baseline_2022.growth: 2022 projected revenue growth: about +2.1%, based on the IBISWorld 2021-2027 projected CAGR.
baseline_2022.profit_margin: 2021 baseline profit margin: 1.8% of revenue; 2026 baseline forecast: 1.9%.
baseline_2022.product_mix: 2021 baseline product mix: almond milk 69.8% of industry revenue, soy milk 10.7%, coconut milk 5.4%, rice milk 2.1%.
baseline_2022.structure: 2021 baseline: 37 enterprises, 63 establishments and 3,947 employees; 2026 baseline forecast: 44 enterprises and 4,611 employees.

how_it_makes_money: Manufacturers buy almonds, soybeans, sweeteners, oils, stabilizers, fortification ingredients and packaging; process them into refrigerated or aseptic shelf-stable beverages; and sell branded, private-label and foodservice products through supermarkets, mass retailers, club stores, natural grocers, convenience channels, coffee chains, broadline distributors and direct account relationships. Premium pricing comes from brand equity, organic and simple-label claims, barista performance, fortification, high-protein positioning, flavor innovation and multi-serve or single-serve packaging.

cost_structure.raw_inputs: Almonds, soybeans, water, sweeteners, oils, flavors, stabilizers, vitamins and minerals are the core variable costs; almond supply is tied heavily to California crop conditions and water costs.
cost_structure.packaging: Cartons, bottles, caps, labels, corrugate and aseptic packaging are significant costs, especially for shelf-stable formats and single-serve products.
cost_structure.manufacturing: Soaking, grinding, filtration, homogenization, heat treatment, aseptic filling, refrigeration, sanitation and quality control drive plant and utility costs.
cost_structure.labor_and_r_and_d: Labor, food-safety compliance, product development and nutrition formulation matter as brands compete on taste, protein, fiber, sugar reduction and clean labels.
cost_structure.distribution: Cold-chain freight, warehousing, slotting, promotions and retail trade spend pressure margins, particularly as category volume softens.
cost_structure.margin_pressure: Retail price premiums versus dairy milk, private-label competition and slower unit sales limit producers' ability to pass through input and logistics inflation.

current_dynamics: The market has split into two tracks. Retail plant-based milk is mature and under pressure, with 2025 dollar sales down 2% and units down 5%, suggesting volume softness and distribution losses despite stable household penetration. Foodservice is expanding faster, with 2025 dollar sales up 16% and pound sales up 14%, because cafes and restaurants use plant-based milks as coffee modifiers and because surcharge removal narrows the effective price gap. Nutrition is becoming a sharper battleground: FDA guidance distinguishes fortified soy beverages from many almond or oat products because fortified soy is closest to dairy milk nutritionally, which gives soy a clearer health and school-meal positioning. Input conditions are mixed: California almond supply remains large but the 2026 crop forecast is slightly lower, while 2026/27 US soybean production is forecast at a record 4.5 billion bushels, easing supply risk for soy-based formulations.
whats_growing: 2025 foodservice plant-based milk sales grew 16% in dollars and 14% in pounds.
2025 plant-based milk retained 38% US household penetration and 75% repeat purchasing among buyer households.
2026 product innovation is moving toward high-protein, complete-protein, fiber-added and nutrient-fortified formats.
2026 soy is regaining relevance as brands launch simple-label soymilk and as FDA nutrition messaging favors fortified soy beverages over many other plant milks.
2025-2026 cafe and barista formats are gaining importance as foodservice becomes a stronger channel than retail.
whats_shrinking: 2025 retail plant-based milk dollar sales declined 2% and unit sales declined 5%.
2025 almond milk remains large but mature; Statista noted Blue Diamond Almond Breeze refrigerated almond milk sales growth of -8.2% in 2025.
2025 retail distribution losses contributed to category declines even though velocity improved in conventional and natural channels.
2026 Danone planned to close its Bridgeton, New Jersey dairy-alternatives facility and shift production to other US plants, reflecting network rationalization.
Soy milk's long-term share remains far below almond milk: the 2021 IBIS baseline had soy at 10.7% of industry revenue versus almond at 69.8%.
recent_developments: Jan. 6, 2025: FDA released draft guidance on naming and labeling plant-based alternatives to animal-derived foods, while continuing to address plant-based milk separately.
May 12, 2025: USDA-NASS forecast the 2025 California almond crop at 2.8 billion pounds, up 3% from 2024.
Dec. 8, 2025: Danone announced a multi-year Big Ten partnership using Oikos and Silk plant-based beverage brands.
Jan. 22, 2026: Califia Farms announced its first soymilk launch as part of its Simple & Organic portfolio.
May 12, 2026: USDA-NASS forecast the 2026 California almond crop at 2.7 billion pounds, down 1% from 2025.
Jul. 15, 2026: Danone expanded Silk Protein with plant-based protein yogurt and shakes after launching Silk Protein milk in January 2026.
outlook: The 2026 outlook is stable to modestly positive rather than high-growth. Retail shelf sales are likely to remain pressured by price premiums, private label and category fatigue, but the base is large and repeat purchasing is resilient. Growth should come from foodservice, protein-fortified soy and blended products, simple-label and organic launches, and products designed for coffee performance. Almond milk should remain the largest revenue pool but will face slower growth and scrutiny over water and nutrition. Soy milk has a better near-term story than it did in the 2022 baseline because fortified soy aligns with federal nutrition guidance and soybean supply looks ample in 2026/27. Margin improvement will depend on manufacturing consolidation, better plant utilization, lower trade spend and disciplined SKU rationalization.
themes: Almond milk scale versus soy nutrition advantage
Premium products versus household value seeking
